obligation.partial_result:
The moment condition itself supplies the protected neighborhood that was formerly assumed. Let \(Q\) be either error law and let \(\phi_Q(t)=\int e^{itu}\,dQ(u)\). Since \(q_e>1\), convexity of \(v\mapsto |v|^{q_e}\), the fact that \(Q\) has total mass one, and the error-moment bound give
\[
 \int |u|\,dQ(u)
 \le \left(\int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ(u)\right)^{1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.
\]
The inequalities \(|1-e^{iv}|\le |v|\) and \(|z|\ge 1-|1-z|\) therefore imply, for every real \(t\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_Q(t)|
 &\ge 1-|1-\phi_Q(t)|\\
 &\ge 1-\int |1-e^{itu}|\,dQ(u)\\
 &\ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Consequently, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},
 \qquad c_*=\frac12,
\]
one has \(\inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\phi_Q(t)|\ge c_*\), uniformly over the enlarged moment class. Thus no separate spectral-modulus restriction is needed.

Two necessary compatibility conditions for the requested fixed density remain. The support and denominator conditions imply
\[
 1=\int_{\mathcal A}f_x(a)\,da
 \ge \int_I f_x(a)\,da
 \ge \kappa |I|.
\]
Moreover, since \(|\mathcal A|=2B_A\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 1=\int_{\mathcal A}f_x(a)\,da
 \le (2B_A)^{1/2}\|f_x\|_2,
\]
and hence
\[
 R_f\ge \|f_x\|_{H^\beta}\ge \|f_x\|_2
 \ge (2B_A)^{-1/2}.
\]
The displayed ranges of the quantitative constants do not themselves impose either \(\kappa|I|\le1\) or \(R_f\ge(2B_A)^{-1/2}\); when either inequality fails, the requested fixed-density subexperiment cannot exist.

Conditional on compatible strict-interior fixed nuisances, moment annihilation gives analytic attenuation. Put \(h_n=f(b_{1,n}-b_{0,n})\), and suppose that
\[
 \int_{\mathcal A}a^k h_n(a)\,da=0,
 \qquad 0\le k<K_n.
\]
For \(|u|\le\Omega\), Taylor's formula for \(e^{iua}\), the support bound \(|a|\le B_A\), and the preceding cancellations yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat h_n(u)|
 &=\left|\int_{\mathcal A}
     \left(e^{iua}-\sum_{k=0}^{K_n-1}\frac{(iua)^k}{k!}\right)
     h_n(a)\,da\right|\\
 &\le \|h_n\|_1 e^{B_A\Omega}
       \frac{(B_A\Omega)^{K_n}}{K_n!}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
By the marked-channel factorization, the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the observed marked-density perturbation equals
\[
 \widehat h_n(s+t)\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t).
\]
For fixed error transforms supported in bounded frequency intervals, this transform is confined to a fixed square and inherits the factorial bound above. What remains unproved is the simultaneous construction of a packet satisfying the Bernoulli range, strict Sobolev slack, and \(K_n^{1/2-\beta}\) supremum separation, together with a weighted chi-square or Hellinger inequality converting the Fourier attenuation into
\[
 \operatorname{TV}\!\left(((P_{0,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n},
 ((P_{1,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n}\right)\le\eta.
\]

prose_updates.tldr: This is a statistical-inference paper about a causal ADRF under two blind nonidentical asymmetric replicates. The fixed quantitative class allows every \(\beta>1/2\) and every fixed \(q_e>1\); the common moment bound itself supplies a uniform protected frequency neighborhood, so no separate local spectral-modulus restriction is imposed. Analytic cocycle identification and an explicit structural response-surface condition establish the causal identifying functional. Two simultaneous bands are distinguished: an explicit finite relaxed outer-sieve construction is uniformly honest and clipped to \(0\le W_n\le2B_Y\), while an abstract noncomputational exact-class construction is uniformly honest with uniformly \(o(1)\) expected maximal width. Neither construction proves the candidate \(r_n\) rate. The fixed-nuisance Bernoulli lower modulus remains unresolved, so there is no matched honest-band rate.

project_justification.gap: Existing statistical results cover blind repeated-measurement density estimation, confidence bands under auxiliary-error, symmetric-error, or fixed-operator designs, and pointwise continuous-treatment inference. They do not provide a quantitative shrinking rate for a uniformly honest simultaneous ADRF band with blind nonidentical asymmetric replicate errors and possible spectral gaps. The present empirical-grid outer set lacks a quantitative marked inverse modulus, and the fixed-nuisance Bernoulli modulus needed for a sharp all-band converse remains unproved.
project_justification.niche: The inferential niche is a nonlinear severe inverse problem over the full Sobolev-continuity range \(\beta>1/2\). Compact treatment support supplies entire transforms, one centered replicate fixes translation, and the uniform \(q_e>1\) moment bound yields \(|\phi_Q(t)|\ge1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}\), hence a common near-origin conditioning region without a separate spectral assumption. The causal target is a stratum-weighted quotient. A jointly measurable response surface driven by an exogenous random element and continuity of the stratum-specific causal mean bridge that observed regression quotient to the point-dose causal curve. The distinction between qualitative identification and quantitative confidence-set diameter is essential here.
project_justification.fill: The paper delivers two inference maps over this enlarged class. The explicit map uses deterministic spline, frequency, truncation, and atomic dimensions; simultaneous probability-, marked-, and mass-channel radii; relaxed compact outer signal sieves; moment-constrained error sieves with the derived protected neighborhood; a joint feasible set; and measurable clipped ADRF extrema. It proves uniform simultaneous coverage and \(0\le W_n\le2B_Y\), but no shrinkage. In parallel, exact empirical-channel residuals are profiled over a compact projected nuisance class with no separately imposed local-modulus constraint. Compactness, expanding-grid equality, and marked cocycle injectivity prove that this abstract exact-class band is uniformly honest and has uniformly \(o(1)\) expected maximal width. The qualitative argument supplies no explicit modulus, and the sharp \(O(r_n)\) upper and matching marked converse remain open.

sampling_model.treatment: \(S_{i1}=A_i+U_{i1}\) and \(S_{i2}=A_i+U_{i2}\), with independent errors that need not be identically distributed or symmetric and may have spectral gaps. The class fixes \(q_e>1\) and \(E|U_j|^{q_e}\le M_e\), and only \(E[U_2]=0\) fixes location. The moment bound implies \(|\phi_j(t)|\ge1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}\), so \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\) give a common protected neighborhood rather than an additional model restriction.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The explicit conservative procedure uses relaxed order-\(d\) B-spline families for \(f_x,q_x\), finite atomic error laws satisfying the \(q_e\)-moment and centering restrictions and the moment-derived protected-neighborhood bounds, and \(p_x\in\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\) against simultaneous empirical probability- and marked-channel restrictions on \(\mathcal D_n\); its outer splines are feasibility devices rather than asserted model laws. A second, abstract procedure profiles the same empirical radii with no approximation allowances over the exact compact projected class \(\mathscr K\), then takes clipped extrema of \(\mu_{\vartheta}\). The latter is an infinite-dimensional existence construction and is not claimed to be computationally implementable.

prose_updates.related_work: Capitao-Miniconi, Gassiat, and Lehéricy provide the unmarked probability-channel cocycle, constrained polynomial estimator, and compact-support \(L^2\) minimax experiment that inform the analytic machinery. Their qualitative H1--H2 identification class has no common error-moment radius and identifies only up to translation; their estimation classes add separate quantitative restrictions, and their Theorem 4 is a latent-density \(L^2\) converse rather than an ADRF-band converse. In the present class, the sole uniform error restriction beyond independence and centering is a fixed \(q_e>1\) moment radius, from which the protected neighborhood is derived. Their rate argument uses a protected-region integrated contrast with nearly parametric forward error and does not supply a Lipschitz inverse for the present grid set whose tolerance contains polynomial Jackson error. Gassiat, Le Corff, and Lehéricy supply the broader analytic-continuation principle for blind deconvolution. Huang and Zhang formulate the error-contaminated continuous-treatment ADRF and derive pointwise inference with a known everywhere-nonzero error transform. Kato and Sasaki (2018) develop deconvolution bands with an unknown error distribution using an auxiliary error sample, together with a symmetric-error repeated-measurement route; that design differs from two blind nonidentical asymmetric replicates and has neither the marked quotient nor joint cell-mass profiling. Kato and Sasaki (2019) obtain multiplier-bootstrap uniform bands under conventional spectral conditions. Kato, Sasaki, and Ura invert Kotlarski restrictions to retain coverage without completeness, but do not establish a shrinking marked-quotient band here. Babii studies honest expected diameter for fixed linear inverse operators. Low supplies a testing-to-expected-length reduction only after a marked modulus is established. None of these sources proves the missing quantitative diameter or fixed-nuisance Bernoulli modulus for the present problem.
prose_updates.interpretation: The observed two-channel law identifies the continuous regression curve \(q_x/f_x\). The common near-zero nonvanishing region used by the cocycle is a consequence of the uniform \(q_e>1\) moment bound, not a separate spectral restriction; open zero sets away from that region remain allowed. Structural exogeneity first equates the regression curve with the stratum-specific causal mean almost everywhere in dose; positivity and continuity then extend the equality to every target dose. Coordinatewise weak unconfoundedness and almost-sure consistency alone would not suffice because they permit treatment-dependent diagonal modifications on null sets.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The causal bridge, moment-derived protected neighborhood, analytic-cocycle identification, simultaneous transform concentration, uniform Jackson approximation for every \(\beta>1/2\), relaxed outer-sieve embedding, and clipped uniform coverage are established. The finite grid-sieve set has no quantitative inverse modulus and therefore no shrinking-width guarantee. Exact-class compactness over the \(q_e>1\) moment class yields a separate uniformly honest band with uniformly \(o(1)\) expected width, but gives no rate, tuning law, or finite algorithm. The sharp-rate program still requires a protected-cube analytic-polynomial confidence construction for both probability and signed marked channels. On the lower side, compatible strict-interior fixed nuisances, a Bernoulli-range Sobolev packet, and a weighted Hellinger or chi-square conversion remain unresolved.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The enlarged fixed quantitative model has compact dose support, bounded outcomes, Sobolev radii with \(\beta>1/2\), overlap, finite-stratum positivity, a fixed \(q_e>1\) error-moment radius, centering of the second error, and the structural causal response surface. It imposes no separate local spectral-modulus restriction: \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\) follow uniformly from the moment bound. The explicit finite relaxed outer-sieve band is uniformly honest for all sufficiently large \(n\) and universally clipped to width at most \(2B_Y\), with no proved shrinkage. The parallel exact-class band is abstract and noncomputational; it is uniformly honest and its expected maximal width is uniformly \(o(1)\), but no explicit rate follows. In particular, no \(O(r_n)\), minimax-matching, or rate-elbow claim is made. The matching-converse kernel remains open as \(\mathrm{oeq{:}fixed\text{-}nuisance\text{-}marked\text{-}modulus}\).

proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(m=|\mathcal X|\) and
\[
 e_{p,n}=\left\{\frac{\log(6m/\alpha)}{2n}\right\}^{1/2}.
\]
We first establish the simultaneous mass event.  If \(Z\) is supported on
\([0,1]\), define
\(\psi(\lambda)=\log E\exp\{\lambda(Z-EZ)\}\).  Boundedness permits
differentiation under exponential tilting, and
\[
 \psi''(\lambda)=\operatorname{Var}_{\lambda}(Z)
 \le E_{\lambda}[(Z-1/2)^2]\le\frac14.
\]
Since \(\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0\), two integrations give
\[
 \log E\exp\{\lambda(Z-EZ)\}\le\frac{\lambda^2}{8},
 \qquad \lambda\in\mathbb R.                                     \tag{1}
\]
For fixed \(x\in\mathcal X\), assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}iid}\) makes
\(\widehat p_x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{X_i=x\}\) the average of
independent Bernoulli variables with mean \(p_x\).  Exponential Markov
inequality applied to (1), with the upper-tail exponent minimized at
\(\lambda=4e_{p,n}\), and the analogous lower-tail calculation give
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 (|\widehat p_x-p_x|>e_{p,n})
 \le2e^{-2ne_{p,n}^2}=\frac{\alpha}{3m}.                           \tag{2}
\]
The union bound over the finite set \(\mathcal X\) yields, uniformly over
\(P\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \left(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|\widehat p_x-p_x|\le e_{p,n}\right)
 \ge1-\frac\alpha3.                                                \tag{3}
\]
Every true mass vector is nonnegative and sums to one, so
\(\mathrm{def{:}mass\text{-}confidence\text{-}region}\) identifies the
event in (3) with
\(\{(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}\in\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\}\).  The asserted
coordinate bound is part of the same definition.

For regular cell counts, let \(N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\).  For
\(t>0\), exponential Markov inequality and \(1+v\le e^v\) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr(N\le np/2)
 &\le e^{tnp/2}E[e^{-tN}]\\
 &=e^{tnp/2}(1-p+pe^{-t})^n\\
 &\le\exp\{tnp/2+np(e^{-t}-1)\}.
 \end{aligned}                                                       \tag{4}
\]
Taking \(t=\log2\) and using \((1-\log2)/2\ge1/8\) gives
\[
 \Pr(N\le np/2)\le e^{-np(1-\log2)/2}\le e^{-np/8}.              \tag{5}
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\) gives \(p_x\ge p_{\min}\), whence
\(\{n_x<np_{\min}/2\}\subseteq\{n_x<np_x/2\}\).  A union bound in (5)
therefore yields
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \left(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x<np_{\min}/2\right)
 \le m e^{-np_{\min}/8}.                                         \tag{6}
\]

It remains to control mass profiling.  Let \(p=(p_x)_x\) and
\(p'=(p'_x)_x\) lie in \(\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\), and fix
\(f_x\in\mathscr F_n\) and \(q_x\in\mathscr Q_n(f_x)\) in every cell.  Put
\[
 e_n=a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}.
\]
The continuum constraints in \(\mathrm{def{:}signal\text{-}sieves}\) give,
for \(a\in I\),
\[
 f_x(a)\ge\kappa/2>0,
 \qquad |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)+e_n.                                 \tag{7}
\]
Thus division is valid, and the definition
\(b_{\mu,n}=4e_n/\kappa\) gives
\[
 \left|\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}\right|
 \le B_Y+\frac{e_n}{f_x(a)}
 \le B_Y+\frac{2e_n}{\kappa}
 =B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2.                                          \tag{8}
\]
The mass-region definition gives
\(|p_x-p'_x|\le|p_x-\widehat p_x|+|p'_x-\widehat p_x|\le2e_{p,n}\).
Consequently
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sup_{a\in I}\left|
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}(p_x-p'_x)\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}\right|
 &\le\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}|p_x-p'_x|
       \sup_{a\in I}\left|\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}\right|\\
 &\le2m\left(B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2\right)e_{p,n}.                \tag{9}
 \end{aligned}
\]

Finally, put \(\gamma=\beta-1/2\).  The corrected declared range gives
\(\gamma>0\).  The tuning definition gives
\(K_n\sim\log n/\log\log n\), while
\(\mathrm{def{:}ecf\text{-}radii}\) gives
\[
 b_{\mu,n}
 =4\kappa^{-1}C_{\beta,\mathcal A}(R_q+B_YR_f)K_n^{-\gamma}
 =O(r_n).                                                           \tag{10}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \log\left(\frac{e_{p,n}}{r_n}\right)
 =-\frac12\log n+\gamma\log\log n
   -\gamma\log\log\log n+O(1)\longrightarrow-\infty.             \tag{11}
\]
All class indices, \(m\), and \(\alpha\) are fixed.  Hence
\(e_{p,n}=o(r_n)\), and (10) implies
\[
 2m\left(B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2\right)e_{p,n}=o(r_n).              \tag{12}
\]
Equations (3), (6), (9), and (12) prove every assertion.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\) and \(x\in\mathcal X\).  Apply
\(\mathrm{lem{:}sobolev\text{-}spline\text{-}jackson}\) first to \(f_x\)
and then to \(q_x\).  The bounds in \(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\)
and \(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), together with the definitions of
\(a_{f,n}\) and \(a_{q,n}\) in \(\mathrm{def{:}ecf\text{-}radii}\), give
order-\(d\) splines \(\widetilde f_{x,n}\) and
\(\widetilde q_{x,n}\) such that
\[
 \|\widetilde f_{x,n}-f_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 \le C_{\beta,\mathcal A}K_n^{1/2-\beta}
       \|f_x\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}
 \le a_{f,n},                                                       \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 \|\widetilde q_{x,n}-q_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 \le C_{\beta,\mathcal A}K_n^{1/2-\beta}
       \|q_x\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}
 \le a_{q,n}.                                                       \tag{2}
\]
The corrected range \(\beta>1/2\) gives \(1/2-\beta<0\).  Since
\(K_n\to\infty\), it follows that \(a_{f,n}\to0\), and therefore
\[
 a_{f,n}<\kappa/2                                                     \tag{3}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).

By definition, \(f_x\) is a nonnegative conditional density.  Assumption
\(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) gives
\(\int_{\mathcal A}f_x(a)\,da=1\).  Equations (1), (3), and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}denominator}\) therefore imply
\[
 \widetilde f_{x,n}(a)\ge-a_{f,n}\quad(a\in\mathcal A),            \tag{4}
\]
\[
 \widetilde f_{x,n}(a)\ge\kappa-a_{f,n}
 =\max\{\kappa/2,\kappa-a_{f,n}\}\quad(a\in I),                   \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 \left|\int_{\mathcal A}\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)\,da-1\right|
 \le\int_{\mathcal A}|\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)-f_x(a)|\,da
 \le2B_Aa_{f,n}.                                                    \tag{6}
\]

We next verify the marked envelope.  The common-event representation in
\(\mathrm{ass{:}structural\text{-}response\text{-}surface}\) takes values
in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\); with \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\), this gives
\(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely.  Conditional Jensen's inequality hence gives
\[
 |m_x(a)|=|E_P[Y\mid A=a,X=x]|\le B_Y
 \quad\text{for }f_x(a)\,da\text{-almost every }a.                  \tag{7}
\]
Because \(q_x=m_xf_x\), equation (7) implies
\(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) Lebesgue-almost everywhere.  This inequality has a
pointwise version under the corrected smoothness range.  Indeed, for either
\(g=f_x\) or \(g=q_x\), the corresponding Sobolev assumption and
\(\beta>1/2\) give
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat g(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
                    |\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty.     \tag{8}
\]
Fourier inversion and dominated convergence supply continuous
representatives of \(f_x\) and \(q_x\).  If
\(|q_x(a_0)|>B_Yf_x(a_0)\) at some \(a_0\), continuity would preserve the
strict inequality on a nonempty interval, contradicting its almost-everywhere
validity.  Hence
\[
 |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\quad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal A.         \tag{9}
\]
Equations (1), (2), and (9) yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)|
 &\le|q_x(a)|+a_{q,n}\\
 &\le B_Y\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)+a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n},
 \qquad a\in\mathcal A.                                           \tag{10}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Equations (4)--(6) are the constraints defining \(\mathscr F_n\), and (10)
is the constraint defining
\(\mathscr Q_n(\widetilde f_{x,n})\).  Thus
\[
 \widetilde f_{x,n}\in\mathscr F_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde q_{x,n}\in\mathscr Q_n(\widetilde f_{x,n}).           \tag{11}
\]

It remains to compare the profiled quotient with the causal estimand.  The
already established \(\mathrm{thm{:}adrf\text{-}id}\) gives
\[
 \mu(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)},
 \qquad a\in I.                                                     \tag{12}
\]
For \(a\in I\), equations (1), (2), and (5), assumption
\(\mathrm{ass{:}denominator}\), and (9) show that every denominator below
is positive and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\frac{\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)}{\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}
       -\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}\right|
 &\le
 \frac{|\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)-q_x(a)|}{\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}
 +\frac{|q_x(a)|\,|\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)-f_x(a)|}
        {f_x(a)\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}\\
 &\le\frac{a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}}{\kappa-a_{f,n}}\\
 &\le2\kappa^{-1}(a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}),                            \tag{13}
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last division uses \(\kappa-a_{f,n}\ge\kappa/2>0\) from (3).
The masses are nonnegative and sum to one, so summing (13) with weights
\(p_x\), using (12), and taking the supremum over \(I\) gives
\[
 \sup_{a\in I}\left|
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x
 \frac{\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)}{\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}-\mu(a)
 \right|
 \le2\kappa^{-1}(a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}).                              \tag{14}
\]
Finally, \(\mathrm{def{:}ecf\text{-}radii}\) defines
\(b_{\mu,n}=4\kappa^{-1}(a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n})\).  Its summands are
nonnegative, so the right-hand side of (14) is at most \(b_{\mu,n}\).

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and a sufficiently large \(n\).
Define the clipped error
\[
 U_j^H=\max\{-H_n,\min\{U_j,H_n\}\}.
\]
On \(\{|U_j|>H_n\}\), one has
\(1\le|U_j|^{q_e}H_n^{-q_e}\).  Thus
\(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\) gives
\[
 P(|U_j|>H_n)
 \le H_n^{-q_e}E_P|U_j|^{q_e}
 \le M_eH_n^{-q_e}.                                                \tag{1}
\]
Since \(U_j^H=U_j\) off this event and two unit-modulus complex numbers are
at distance at most two, for every real \(t\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |E_Pe^{itU_j^H}-\phi_j(t)|
 &\le E_P|e^{itU_j^H}-e^{itU_j}|\\
 &\le2P(|U_j|>H_n)
 \le2M_eH_n^{-q_e}=\tau_{e,n}.                                    \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Clipping does not increase absolute value, so
\[
 E_P|U_j^H|^{q_e}\le E_P|U_j|^{q_e}\le M_e.                       \tag{3}
\]
For \(j=2\), the first moment exists by
\(\mathrm{lem{:}moment\text{-}derived\text{-}local\text{-}modulus}\).
Consequently the centering identity in \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\)
may be subtracted from the clipped mean.  Since \(q_e>1\),
\(|U_2|\le H_n^{1-q_e}|U_2|^{q_e}\) on \(\{|U_2|>H_n\}\), and hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |E_PU_2^H|
 &=|E_P(U_2^H-U_2)|\\
 &\le E_P\{|U_2|\mathbf1(|U_2|>H_n)\}\\
 &\le H_n^{1-q_e}E_P|U_2|^{q_e}
 \le M_eH_n^{1-q_e}.                                               \tag{4}
 \end{aligned}
\]
This is the step that requires the strict threshold \(q_e>1\); it also
shows that the centering tolerance tends to zero because \(H_n\to\infty\).

We next replace the law of \(U_j^H\), supported on \([-H_n,H_n]\), by an
atomic law preserving the grid values and the two displayed moments.  Put
\[
 D=2|\Gamma_n|+2
\]
and define the continuous map
\[
 v(u)=\left(
 (\operatorname{Re}e^{itu},\operatorname{Im}e^{itu})_{t\in\Gamma_n},
 u,|u|^{q_e}\right)\in\mathbb R^D.                                \tag{5}
\]
Finite simple-function approximations to the law of \(U_j^H\) have
\(v\)-expectations in the convex hull of the compact set
\(v([-H_n,H_n])\), and uniform continuity of \(v\) makes these expectations
converge to \(E_Pv(U_j^H)\).  Thus this vector lies in the closure of the
convex hull.

We show that the convex hull is closed and obtain the support bound at the
same time.  If a finite convex representation uses more than \(D+1\)
locations \(u_r\), its augmented vectors
\((1,v(u_r))\in\mathbb R^{D+1}\) are linearly dependent.  Hence there are
real coefficients \(a_r\), not all zero, such that
\[
 \sum_ra_r=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_ra_rv(u_r)=0.                                                \tag{6}
\]
After changing all signs if necessary, some \(a_r>0\).  For weights \(w_r\),
put
\[
 c=\min_{r:a_r>0}\frac{w_r}{a_r}>0,
 \qquad w'_r=w_r-ca_r.
\]
Equation (6) shows that the new weights have the same sum and barycenter,
remain nonnegative, and make at least one positive-weight location vanish.
Iteration leaves at most
\[
 D+1=2|\Gamma_n|+3\le M_n                                         \tag{7}
\]
locations.  It follows that the entire convex hull is the image of the
compact product of the \(D\)-simplex and \(D+1\) copies of
\([-H_n,H_n]\) under the continuous barycenter map.  It is therefore compact
and closed.  The preceding limit argument proves that \(E_Pv(U_j^H)\) is in
that convex hull, and (7) provides a representation using at most \(D+1\)
locations.

Let \(\bar Q_{j,n}\) be the resulting atomic law.  Order its locations and
pad the representation with zero-weight atoms at \(H_n\).  By (5), its
characteristic function \(\bar\phi_{j,n}\) agrees with that of \(U_j^H\) at
every \(t\in\Gamma_n\), its mean is \(E_PU_j^H\), its support lies in
\([-H_n,H_n]\), and
\[
 \int|u|^{q_e}\,d\bar Q_{j,n}(u)
 =E_P|U_j^H|^{q_e}\le M_e.                                        \tag{8}
\]
Exact grid agreement and (2) give
\[
 \max_{t\in\Gamma_n}|\bar\phi_{j,n}(t)-\phi_j(t)|
 \le\tau_{e,n}.                                                    \tag{9}
\]
For \(j=2\), preservation of the mean and (4) give
\[
 \left|\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_n}w_{2\ell}u_{2\ell}\right|
 \le M_eH_n^{1-q_e}
 \le2M_eH_n^{1-q_e}.                                               \tag{10}
\]

It remains to check the protected-frequency clause of the corrected
\(\mathrm{def{:}error\text{-}sieves}\).  Apply
\(\mathrm{lem{:}moment\text{-}derived\text{-}local\text{-}modulus}\) to
\(\bar Q_{j,n}\), using (8).  It gives directly
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\bar\phi_{j,n}(t)|\ge c_*\ge c_*/2.            \tag{11}
\]
Thus no grid interpolation and no independent spectral assumption are used.
Equations (8) and (11), together with the support and ordered-atom
construction, show \(\bar\phi_{j,n}\in\widetilde\Phi_{j,n}\).  In the
second coordinate, (10) verifies the additional centering tolerance, so
\(\bar\phi_{2,n}\in\Phi_{2,n}\); in the first coordinate,
\(\Phi_{1,n}=\widetilde\Phi_{1,n}\).  Equations (9)--(10) prove the claim.

Fix a sufficiently large \(n\).  We first establish the simultaneous
confidence event.  Conditional on \((X_i)_{i=1}^n\), assumption
\(\mathrm{ass{:}iid}\) makes the observations in each nonempty cell
independent with the conditional law given \(X=x\).  Each real and imaginary
part of a probability-channel summand lies in \([-1,1]\).  The common-event
response representation in \(\mathrm{def{:}model\text{-}class}\), together
with \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\), gives \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely, so
each real and imaginary part of a marked-channel summand lies in
\([-B_Y,B_Y]\).

Apply the moment-generating-function calculation in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\), after rescaling an interval of
length \(2c\), separately to real and imaginary parts.  Since
\(|z|>u\) implies
\(\max\{|\operatorname{Re}z|,|\operatorname{Im}z|\}>u/\sqrt2\), when
\(n_x>\lambda_n\), for each \((s,t)\in\mathcal D_n\),
\[
 \Pr\left(
 |\widehat F_{x,n}(s,t)-F_x(s,t)|
 >2\sqrt{\lambda_n/n_x}\ \middle|\ (X_i)_{i=1}^n
 \right)\le4e^{-\lambda_n},                                       \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 \Pr\left(
 |\widehat G_{x,n}(s,t)-G_x(s,t)|
 >2B_Y\sqrt{\lambda_n/n_x}\ \middle|\ (X_i)_{i=1}^n
 \right)\le4e^{-\lambda_n}.                                       \tag{2}
\]
If \(n_x\le\lambda_n\), the empirical-channel definitions, including the
empty-cell convention, and \(|F_x|\le1\), \(|G_x|\le B_Y\) show
deterministically that the deviations are at most
\(\rho^F_{x,n}=2\) and \(\rho^G_{x,n}=2B_Y\).  A conditional union bound
over both channels, every cell, and every grid point has failure probability
at most
\[
 8|\mathcal X||\mathcal D_n|e^{-\lambda_n}=\alpha/6.               \tag{3}
\]
Combining (3) with the mass-region failure probability \(\alpha/3\) from
\(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\), and integrating over the labels,
gives, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha})
 \ge1-\alpha/3-\alpha/6\ge1-\alpha.                               \tag{4}
\]

Suppose now that \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\) occurs.  Apply
\(\mathrm{lem{:}outer\text{-}spline\text{-}embedding}\) in every cell and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}atomic\text{-}grid\text{-}embedding}\) to both error laws.
Define
\[
 \bar\theta_n=
 \bigl((p_x,\widetilde f_{x,n},\widetilde q_{x,n})_{x\in\mathcal X},
       \bar\phi_{1,n},\bar\phi_{2,n}\bigr).
\]
The event puts its mass vector in \(\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\).  At a point
\((s,t)\in\mathcal D_n\), both \(s\) and \(t\) belong to \(\Gamma_n\).
Characteristic functions have modulus at most one.  Furthermore,
\(|\widehat f_x(u)|\le1\), and equations (7)--(9) of the outer-embedding
proof give \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\), so
\(|\widehat q_x(u)|\le\int|q_x|\le B_Y\).  Uniform approximation on the
interval \(\mathcal A\), of length \(2B_A\), gives
\[
 |\widehat{\widetilde f}_{x,n}(u)-\widehat f_x(u)|
 \le2B_Aa_{f,n},
 \qquad
 |\widehat{\widetilde q}_{x,n}(u)-\widehat q_x(u)|
 \le2B_Aa_{q,n}.                                                    \tag{5}
\]
At grid points, the atomic embedding and the triangle inequality give
\[
 |\bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t)|
 \le|\bar\phi_{1,n}(s)-\phi_1(s)|
   +|\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-\phi_2(t)|
 \le2\tau_{e,n}.                                                    \tag{6}
\]
The established factorization lemma, (5)--(6), and the triangle inequality
therefore imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat{\widetilde f}_{x,n}(s+t)
   \bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-F_x(s,t)|
 &\le2B_Aa_{f,n}+2\tau_{e,n}\le\delta^F_n,\\
 |\widehat{\widetilde q}_{x,n}(s+t)
   \bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-G_x(s,t)|
 &\le2B_Aa_{q,n}+2B_Y\tau_{e,n}\le\delta^G_n.                    \tag{7}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Combining (7) with the empirical inequalities defining
\(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\) verifies every residual constraint in
\(\mathrm{def{:}joint\text{-}feasible\text{-}set}\); the two embedding
lemmas verify the deterministic sieve constraints.  Hence
\[
 \bar\theta_n\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}.                                 \tag{8}
\]
The quotient conclusion of the outer-embedding lemma, with the true mass
vector, gives
\[
 \|\mu_{\bar\theta_n}-\mu\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le b_{\mu,n}.           \tag{9}
\]

Finally, consider an arbitrary realized sample; this step does not use the
confidence event.  Put \(e_n=a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}\).  For any
\(\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}\), the simplex constraint, the marked outer
envelope, and \(f_x\ge\kappa/2\) on \(I\) yield
\[
 |\mu_\theta(a)|
 \le\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x
 \left(B_Y+\frac{e_n}{f_x(a)}\right)
 \le B_Y+\frac{2e_n}{\kappa}
 =B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2.                                          \tag{10}
\]
If the feasible set is nonempty, put
\(\ell(a)=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)\) and
\(u(a)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)\).  From (10) and
\(\ell(a)\le u(a)\),
\[
 \ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\le B_Y,
 \quad -B_Y\le u(a)+b_{\mu,n},
 \quad \ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\le u(a)+b_{\mu,n}.                      \tag{11}
\]
Together with \(-B_Y\le B_Y\), these pairwise inequalities imply
\[
 \max\{-B_Y,\ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\}
 \le\min\{B_Y,u(a)+b_{\mu,n}\}.
\]
Both endpoints lie in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\).  If the feasible set is empty, both
endpoints are zero by \(\mathrm{def{:}profiled\text{-}band}\).  Thus, for
every sample,
\[
 L_n(a)\le U_n(a)\quad(a\in I),
 \qquad 0\le W_n\le2B_Y.                                          \tag{12}
\]
Equations (4), (8), (9), and (12) prove the stated concentration,
outer-embedding, ADRF-approximation, and clipping conclusions.  No inverse
diameter or quantitative shrinking-width assertion is used.

added_lemmas.statement:
For every \(\beta>1/2\), let \(d=\lceil\beta\rceil+1\).  For every
\(g\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\), the uniform order-\(d\) B-spline spaces on
\(\mathcal A\) satisfy, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 \inf_{s\in\operatorname{span}\{\mathsf B_{k,K_n}:1\le k\le K_n+d\}}
 \|g-s\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 \le C_{\beta,\mathcal A}K_n^{1/2-\beta}
       \|g\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}.
\]
The constant \(C_{\beta,\mathcal A}<\infty\) is independent of \(g\),
\(n\), and the spline coefficients.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(h=2B_A/K_n\).  Since \(K_n\to\infty\) by
\(\mathrm{def{:}upper\text{-}tuning\text{-}grid}\), it suffices to consider
\(0<h\le1\).  Use the Fourier convention
\[
 \widehat g(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{ita}g(a)\,da,
 \qquad
 g(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ita}\widehat g(t)\,dt.
\]
The inversion formula holds for the continuous representative of \(g\):
because \(\beta>1/2\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat g(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
                    |\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty.       \tag{1}
\]
Define
\[
 g_h(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{|t|\le h^{-1}}
          e^{-ita}\widehat g(t)\,dt.
\]
Another application of Cauchy--Schwarz, followed by
\(\int_{h^{-1}}^\infty t^{-2\beta}\,dt
=(2\beta-1)^{-1}h^{2\beta-1}\), yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|g-g_h\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}
 &\le \frac1{2\pi}
 \left\{\int_{|t|>h^{-1}}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
                    |\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}\\
 &\le C_1(\beta)h^{\beta-1/2}\|g\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}.            \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The division by \(2\beta-1\) is valid exactly under the declared condition
\(\beta>1/2\).

We next establish the smooth-function approximation used below.  Fix the
clamped normalized B-spline basis specified in
\(\mathrm{def{:}signal\text{-}sieves}\).  Its elements are nonnegative,
form a partition of unity on \(\mathcal A\), and span the order-\(d\) spline
space on the uniform partition.  In particular, that space contains every
polynomial of degree at most \(d-1\).  For each basis index \(k\), choose a
point \(\xi_k\) in the support of \(\mathsf B_{k,K_n}\).  If
\(v\in C^d(\mathbb R)\), let \(\Lambda_{k,h}(v)\) be the \(k\)-th B-spline
coefficient of the degree-\((d-1)\) Taylor polynomial of \(v\) at \(\xi_k\).
After translation and dilation by \(h\), there is one interior coefficient
pattern and only finitely many boundary patterns.  Finite-dimensional norm
equivalence for these finitely many patterns gives a constant \(C_d\),
independent of \(h\), \(k\), and \(v\), such that
\[
 |\Lambda_{k,h}(v)|
 \le C_d\max_{0\le j\le d-1}h^j|v^{(j)}(\xi_k)|.                    \tag{3}
\]
Define
\[
 (J_hv)(a)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_n+d}
              \Lambda_{k,h}(v)\mathsf B_{k,K_n}(a).
\]
If \(p\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(d-1\), its Taylor polynomial
of that order at every \(\xi_k\) is \(p\) itself.  Hence \(J_hp=p\).
For fixed \(a\in\mathcal A\), let \(p_a\) be the degree-\((d-1)\) Taylor
polynomial of \(v\) at \(a\).  Whenever
\(\mathsf B_{k,K_n}(a)\ne0\), locality of the order-\(d\) basis gives
\(|\xi_k-a|\le C_dh\).  Taylor's formula with integral remainder then gives,
for \(0\le j\le d-1\),
\[
 h^j|(v-p_a)^{(j)}(\xi_k)|
 \le C_dh^d\|v^{(d)}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}.                     \tag{4}
\]
Since \((v-p_a)(a)=0\), polynomial reproduction, (3), (4), nonnegativity,
and the partition of unity imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |v(a)-J_hv(a)|
 &=|J_h(v-p_a)(a)|\\
 &\le \sum_k\mathsf B_{k,K_n}(a)
          |\Lambda_{k,h}(v-p_a)|\\
 &\le C_dh^d\|v^{(d)}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}.                    \tag{5}
 \end{aligned}
\]

Apply (5) to \(v=g_h\).  Differentiation under the compact-frequency
integral and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|g_h^{(d)}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}
 &\le \frac1{2\pi}
 \left\{\int_{|t|\le h^{-1}}|t|^{2d}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
                    |\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}\\
 &\le C_2(\beta,d)h^{\beta-d-1/2}
       \|g\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}.                                \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]
For the last inequality, split the first integral at one and use
\(d=\lceil\beta\rceil+1>\beta\), so
\(\int_1^{h^{-1}}t^{2d-2\beta}\,dt
\le C(\beta,d)h^{-(2d-2\beta+1)}\).  Combining (2), (5), and (6) gives
the spline \(s=J_hg_h\) with
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|g-s\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 &\le C_3(\beta,d)h^{\beta-1/2}\|g\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}\\
 &=C_3(\beta,d)(2B_A)^{\beta-1/2}K_n^{1/2-\beta}
       \|g\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}.                                \tag{7}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The function \(s\) lies in the span displayed in the statement by the basis
definition.  Taking the fixed constant \(C_{\beta,\mathcal A}\) no smaller
than the constant in (7) proves the claimed uniform Jackson inequality.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and let \(Q_j\) be a Borel probability law on
\(\mathbb R\) such that
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e,
 \qquad
 \phi_{Q_j}(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itu}\,dQ_j(u).
\]
For \(q_e>1\),
\[
 \int_{mathbb R}|u|\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e^{1/q_e},
 \qquad
 |\phi_{Q_j}(s)-\phi_{Q_j}(t)|
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}|s-t|,
\]
and
\[
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.
\]
Consequently, for \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\),
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge c_*.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Because \(q_e>1\), H\"older's inequality with respect to the probability
measure \(Q_j\) gives
\[
 \int_{mathbb R}|u|\,dQ_j(u)
 \le
 \left\{\int_{mathbb R}|u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\right\}^{1/q_e}
 \left\{\int_{mathbb R}1\,dQ_j(u)\right\}^{1-1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.                                                   \tag{1}
\]
For real \(v\), the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to
\(r\mapsto e^{irv}\) gives \(|e^{iv}-1|\le|v|\).  Hence, for all real
\(s,t\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_{Q_j}(s)-\phi_{Q_j}(t)|
 &\le\int_{\mathbb R}|e^{isu}-e^{itu}|\,dQ_j(u)\\
 &\le|s-t|\int_{\mathbb R}|u|\,dQ_j(u)
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}|s-t|.                                             \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\phi_{Q_j}(0)=1\), the reverse triangle inequality and (2) yield
\[
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|
 \ge1-|\phi_{Q_j}(t)-\phi_{Q_j}(0)|
 \ge1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                              \tag{3}
\]
The positivity of \(M_e\) makes
\(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}>0\).  If \(|t|\le\nu_*\), then (3) gives
\[
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge1-\nu_*M_e^{1/q_e}=\frac12=c_*.
\]
This proves all assertions.

proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\textnormal{def:exact-projected-class}\), every signal coordinate is
supported in the common compact interval
\(\mathcal A=[-B_A,B_A]\), and its \(H^\beta\)-norm is bounded by \(R_f\)
or \(R_q\).  Use the Fourier norm convention
\[
 \|g\|_{H^\beta}^2
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
       |\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Fourier inversion and Cauchy--Schwarz give, initially for smooth functions and
then by approximation in \(H^\beta\),
\[
 |g(a)|
 \le \frac{\|g\|_{H^\beta}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
       \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}, \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 |g(a)-g(b)|
 \le \frac{\|g\|_{H^\beta}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}|e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}|^2
                 (1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}.             \tag{3}
\]
The integral in (2) is finite precisely because the enlarged class has
\(\beta>1/2\).  In (3), the integrand tends pointwise to zero as
\(|a-b|\to0\) and is bounded by the integrable function
\(4(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\).  Dominated convergence therefore gives a common
modulus of continuity for every fixed-radius Sobolev ball.  Thus each such
ball is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on \(\mathcal A\).

For completeness, these estimates give total boundedness directly.  Given
\(\epsilon>0\), choose a finite spatial mesh of \(\mathcal A\) such that the
common modulus in (3) is at most \(\epsilon/4\) between any point and a
nearest mesh point.  Partition the bounded range furnished by (2) into
finitely many intervals of length at most \(\epsilon/2\).  If two functions
have values in the same interval at every mesh point, then their uniform
distance is at most
\(\epsilon/4+\epsilon/2+\epsilon/4=\epsilon\).  Selecting one representative
from each nonempty pattern gives a finite uniform \(\epsilon\)-net.

We next prove closedness in the uniform metric.  Suppose that
\(g_m\) is supported in \(\mathcal A\),
\(\|g_m\|_{H^\beta}\le R\), and \(g_m\to g\) uniformly on
\(\mathcal A\).  The continuous representative of every \(g_m\) is zero off
\(\mathcal A\), hence is zero at the boundary of \(\mathcal A\).  The zero
extension of \(g\) is consequently continuous and
\[
 \|g_m-g\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}
 \le (2B_A)^{1/2}\|g_m-g\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 \longrightarrow0.                                               \tag{4}
\]
Set \(h_m(t)=(1+t^2)^{\beta/2}\widehat g_m(t)\).  Equation (1) makes
\((h_m)\) bounded in the Hilbert space \(L^2(\mathbb R)\).  Expanding in a
countable orthonormal basis and applying diagonal selection gives a subsequence
\(h_{m_k}\rightharpoonup h\) such that
\[
 \|h\|_2\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|h_{m_k}\|_2.                    \tag{5}
\]
By (4) and the Fourier isometry,
\(\widehat g_{m_k}\to\widehat g\) strongly in \(L^2\).  Multiplication by
\((1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}\) is bounded on \(L^2\), so the weak convergence also
implies
\[
 \widehat g_{m_k}\rightharpoonup(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h.
\]
Uniqueness of the weak limit gives
\(\widehat g=(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h\).  Hence \(g\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\),
and (5) gives \(\|g\|_{H^\beta}\le R\).  The fixed-support Sobolev ball is
therefore closed in the complete space \(C(\mathcal A)\).  Together with
total boundedness, this proves its compactness in uniform distance.

Apply this conclusion at radii \(R_f\) and \(R_q\).  Uniform convergence on
the common support preserves nonnegativity, the lower bound by \(\kappa\) on
\(I\), and the domination \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\).  It also preserves the unit
integral because
\[
 \left|\int_{\mathcal A}(f_m-f)\right|
 \le2B_A\|f_m-f\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\longrightarrow0.         \tag{6}
\]
Thus the joint signal subset in \(\mathscr K\) is closed in a finite product
of compact spaces and is compact.  The mass vectors form a closed subset of
the finite-dimensional simplex, by \(p_x\ge p_{\min}\) and
\(\sum_xp_x=1\), and hence are compact as well.

It remains to treat an error-law coordinate.  Let \((Q_m)\) satisfy the
common \(q_e\)-moment bound.  Since
\(\mathbf 1\{|u|>R\}\le |u|^{q_e}R^{-q_e}\),
\[
 \sup_m Q_m(|u|>R)\le M_eR^{-q_e}.                                 \tag{7}
\]
This proves tightness directly.  To exhibit a weakly convergent subsequence,
diagonally select the distribution functions at the rational numbers.  The
monotone rational limits, made right-continuous by taking infima over rationals
strictly to the right, define a distribution function; (7) forces its limits
at negative and positive infinity to be zero and one.  Rational sandwiching
then gives convergence at every continuity point of the limiting distribution
function.  For a bounded continuous function, truncate to \([-R,R]\) using
(7), partition that interval at continuity points, and use uniform continuity
on each partition.  First refining the partition and then sending
\(R\to\infty\) proves weak convergence, along the selected subsequence, to a
Borel probability law \(Q\):
\[
 \int h\,dQ_m\longrightarrow\int h\,dQ
 \quad\text{for every bounded continuous }h.                      \tag{8}
\]

For every finite \(L\), the function \(|u|^{q_e}\wedge L\) is bounded and
continuous.  Equation (8) and monotone convergence in \(L\) give
\[
 \int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ(u)
 =\sup_L\int(|u|^{q_e}\wedge L)\,dQ(u)\le M_e.                   \tag{9}
\]
The enlarged error class assumes \(q_e>1\), and this strict inequality is
used in
\[
 \int_{|u|>R}|u|\,dQ_m(u)
 \le R^{1-q_e}\int|u|^{q_e}\,dQ_m(u)
 \le M_eR^{1-q_e}\longrightarrow0,                               \tag{10}
\]
uniformly in \(m\); (9) gives the same bound for \(Q\).  Apply (8) to the
identity clipped to \([-R,R]\), use (10), and then send \(R\to\infty\).
The first moments converge.  Consequently the restriction
\(\int u\,dQ_2(u)=0\) is closed.  Equations (7)--(10) prove compactness of
each error-law coordinate in any metric that metrizes weak convergence.  No
spectral-modulus restriction has been used or is part of the corrected exact
class.

The same moment calculation and the power-mean inequality give
\(\int|u|\,dQ_m(u)\le M_e^{1/q_e}\).  Therefore
\[
 |\phi_{Q_m}(s)-\phi_{Q_m}(t)|
 \le\int|e^{isu}-e^{itu}|\,dQ_m(u)
 \le |s-t|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                            \tag{11}
\]
Weak convergence gives pointwise convergence of the characteristic functions
by (8).  Covering a fixed compact frequency interval by a finite mesh and
using (11) for both \(Q_m\) and \(Q\) upgrades pointwise convergence to
uniform convergence on that interval.  Combining the mass, signal, and two
error coordinates proves compactness of \(\mathscr K\).

Now let \(\vartheta_m\to\vartheta\) in the asserted product metric.  Uniform
signal convergence and common support imply
\[
 \sup_{r\in\mathbb R}|\widehat f_{x,m}(r)-\widehat f_x(r)|
 \le2B_A\|f_{x,m}-f_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\longrightarrow0,  \tag{12}
\]
and the same inequality holds for \(q_x\).  Characteristic functions have
modulus at most one, while \(\int f_x=1\) and
\(\int|q_x|\le B_Y\int f_x=B_Y\).  Thus (11)--(12) imply local uniform
convergence on \(\mathbb R^2\) of both fitted channels
\[
 (s,t)\longmapsto\widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t),
 \qquad
 (s,t)\longmapsto\widehat q_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t).    \tag{13}
\]

For continuity of the profiled target, the bounds
\(f_x,f'_x\ge\kappa\) on \(I\) and \(|q'_x|\le B_Yf'_x\) yield
\[
 \left\|\frac{q_x}{f_x}-\frac{q'_x}{f'_x}\right\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le\kappa^{-1}\|q_x-q'_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
    +B_Y\kappa^{-1}\|f_x-f'_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}.        \tag{14}
\]
Also \(\|q'_x/f'_x\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le B_Y\).  Hence
\[
 \|\mu_\vartheta-\mu_{\vartheta'}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le\sum_xp_x
       \left\|\frac{q_x}{f_x}-\frac{q'_x}{f'_x}\right\|_{L^\infty(I)}
      +B_Y\sum_x|p_x-p'_x|,                                      \tag{15}
\]
which tends to zero in the product metric.  This proves continuity from
\(\mathscr K\) to \(C(I)\).

Finally fix \(n\) and a realized sample \(z\).  By
\(\textnormal{def:exact-joint-feasible-set}\), feasibility is the conjunction
of finitely many mass and channel inequalities.  The corresponding positive
part violations include
\[
 v^F_{x,s,t}(z,\vartheta)
 =\left(
 \left|\widehat F_{x,n}(z;s,t)
       -\widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t)\right|
       -\rho^F_{x,n}(z)
 \right)_+,                                                     \tag{16}
\]
the analogous \(v^G_{x,s,t}\), and
\[
 v^p_x(z,\vartheta)
 =\left(
 |p_x-\widehat p_x(z)|
 -\left\{\frac{\log(6|\mathcal X|/\alpha)}{2n}\right\}^{1/2}
 \right)_+.                                                     \tag{17}
\]
The empirical sums, counts, empty-cell convention, and radii in
\(\textnormal{def:mass-confidence-region}\),
\(\textnormal{def:upper-tuning-grid}\), and
\(\textnormal{def:ecf-radii}\) are Borel measurable functions of \(z\).
Thus (16)--(17) are measurable in \(z\).  Equations (13) and continuity of
the mass coordinates show that they are continuous in \(\vartheta\).  Their
common zero set is exactly \(\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)\), so it is
closed in compact \(\mathscr K\), and therefore compact.  This also proves
the asserted measurability and continuity of all constraint-violation
functions.

Suppose, to the contrary, that (1) does not tend to zero.  Then there are
\(\epsilon>0\), integers \(n_k\to\infty\), realized samples \(z_k\) with
\(\min_x n_x(z_k)\ge n_kp_{\min}/2\), and tuples
\(\vartheta_k,\vartheta'_k\in
\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n_k,\alpha}(z_k)\) such that
\[
 \|\mu_{\vartheta_k}-\mu_{\vartheta'_k}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \ge\epsilon.                                                    \tag{2}
\]
By \(\textnormal{lem:exact-class-compactness}\), after passage to one common
subsequence,
\[
 \vartheta_k\longrightarrow\vartheta,
 \qquad
 \vartheta'_k\longrightarrow\vartheta'                           \tag{3}
\]
in the product topology of that lemma.

Both mass vectors belong to the same region from
\(\textnormal{def:mass-confidence-region}\), whence
\[
 \max_{x\in\mathcal X}|p_{x,k}-p'_{x,k}|
 \le2\left\{\frac{\log(6|\mathcal X|/\alpha)}{2n_k}\right\}^{1/2}
 \longrightarrow0.                                                \tag{4}
\]
The two limiting mass vectors are therefore equal.  From
\(\textnormal{def:upper-tuning-grid}\),
\[
 |\mathcal D_n|=(2K_n^2+1)^2,
 \qquad
 \lambda_n=O(\log K_n)=o(n).                                     \tag{5}
\]
The regular-count condition and \(\textnormal{def:ecf-radii}\) consequently
give
\[
 \max_x\rho^F_{x,n_k}
 \le2\left(\frac{2\lambda_{n_k}}{n_kp_{\min}}\right)^{1/2}=o(1),
 \qquad
 \max_x\rho^G_{x,n_k}
 \le B_Y\max_x\rho^F_{x,n_k}=o(1).                              \tag{6}
\]

For a tuple \(\vartheta\), abbreviate its fitted channels by
\[
 F_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)
 =\widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t),
 \qquad
 G_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)
 =\widehat q_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t).                    \tag{7}
\]
The moment constraint in \(\textnormal{def:exact-projected-class}\) and the
power-mean inequality give
\(\int|u|\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e^{1/q_e}\).  Since \(|a|\le B_A\) on
\(\mathcal A\), \(|e^{iv}-e^{iw}|\le|v-w|\), and
\(\int|q_x|\le B_Y\), direct integration of the product laws gives, uniformly
over \(\vartheta\in\mathscr K\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |F_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)-F_{x,\vartheta}(s',t')|
 &\le(B_A+M_e^{1/q_e})(|s-s'|+|t-t'|),\\
 |G_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)-G_{x,\vartheta}(s',t')|
 &\le B_Y(B_A+M_e^{1/q_e})(|s-s'|+|t-t'|).
 \end{aligned}                                                    \tag{8}
\]
At each grid point, feasibility around the same empirical transform and the
triangle inequality imply
\[
 |F_{x,\vartheta_k}-F_{x,\vartheta'_k}|\le2\rho^F_{x,n_k},
 \qquad
 |G_{x,\vartheta_k}-G_{x,\vartheta'_k}|\le2\rho^G_{x,n_k}.         \tag{9}
\]
The mesh of \(\Gamma_{n_k}\) is \((B_AK_{n_k})^{-1}\), while its range is
\(K_{n_k}/B_A\to\infty\).  For any fixed \((s,t)\), take a nearest grid
point for all sufficiently large \(k\).  Equations (6), (8), and (9) show
that the difference between the two probability channels, and separately
between the two marked channels, tends to zero at \((s,t)\).  Local uniform
channel convergence from \(\textnormal{lem:exact-class-compactness}\) permits
passage to (3), giving
\[
 F_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)=F_{x,\vartheta'}(s,t),
 \qquad
 G_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)=G_{x,\vartheta'}(s,t)                       \tag{10}
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) and every \((s,t)\in\mathbb R^2\).

We now derive the required local nonvanishing from the moment restriction;
no spectral-modulus hypothesis is used.  For any error law in the corrected
exact class,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_Q(v)|
 &\ge1-|\phi_Q(v)-1|\\
 &\ge1-\int|e^{ivu}-1|\,dQ(u)\\
 &\ge1-|v|\int|u|\,dQ(u)
 \ge1-|v|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                             \tag{11}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},\qquad c_*=1/2,                        \tag{12}
\]
every candidate error characteristic function has modulus at least \(c_*\)
on \([-\nu_*,\nu_*]\).  Also, for every candidate density,
\[
 |\widehat f_x(v)-1|
 \le\int_{\mathcal A}|e^{iva}-1|f_x(a)\,da
 \le B_A|v|.                                                      \tag{13}
\]
Put \(\delta=\min\{(4B_A)^{-1},\nu_*/2\}>0\).  Equations (11)--(13)
show that, for \(|u|,|t|\le\delta\), every factor of
\(F_{x,\vartheta}(u,t)\) and \(F_{x,\vartheta'}(u,t)\) is nonzero.

Fix \(x\), and denote the signal coordinates of \(\vartheta'\) by
\(\widetilde f_x,\widetilde q_x\).  Because \(q_e>1\), both second-coordinate
error laws have finite first moments, so their characteristic functions are
differentiable at zero.  Centering in
\(\textnormal{def:exact-projected-class}\) gives
\[
 \phi'_{Q_2}(0)=i\int u\,dQ_2(u)=0,
 \qquad
 \phi'_{Q'_2}(0)=i\int u\,dQ'_2(u)=0.                             \tag{14}
\]
Differentiate the first equality in (10) with respect to \(t\) at
\((u,0)\), divide by the common nonzero channel value, and use (14).  For
\(|u|\le\delta\),
\[
 \frac{\widehat f'_x(u)}{\widehat f_x(u)}
 =\left.\frac{\partial_tF_{x,\vartheta}(u,t)}
 {F_{x,\vartheta}(u,t)}\right|_{t=0}
 =\left.\frac{\partial_tF_{x,\vartheta'}(u,t)}
 {F_{x,\vartheta'}(u,t)}\right|_{t=0}
 =\frac{\widehat{\widetilde f}'_x(u)}
        {\widehat{\widetilde f}_x(u)}.                            \tag{15}
\]
The derivative of
\(\widehat f_x/\widehat{\widetilde f}_x\) is consequently zero on this
interval.  Since both transforms equal one at zero,
\[
 \widehat f_x(u)=\widehat{\widetilde f}_x(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.                                             \tag{16}
\]

Compact support makes both transforms entire: differentiation of every order
under the integral is justified by
\(|a|\le B_A\) and
\(|e^{iza}|\le e^{B_A|\operatorname{Im}z|}\).  Applied to their difference,
(16) makes every derivative at zero vanish.  Its everywhere-convergent Taylor
series is therefore zero, so the two transforms agree on all of \(\mathbb C\).
To verify injectivity without invoking an undeclared Fourier-uniqueness result,
let \(h=f_x-\widetilde f_x\) and let \(\gamma_\sigma\) be the centered
Gaussian density of variance \(\sigma^2\).  Absolute integrability and the
Gaussian integral give
\[
 (h*\gamma_\sigma)(a)
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ita}
   \widehat h(t)e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}\,dt=0.                         \tag{17}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \|h*\gamma_\sigma-h\|_1
 \le\int\gamma_\sigma(y)\|h(\,\cdot-y)-h\|_1\,dy
 \longrightarrow0.                                              \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, translation continuity holds first for indicators of bounded
intervals, then for their finite linear combinations, and finally for every
\(L^1\) function by approximation; the integrand in (18) is bounded by
\(2\|h\|_1\), and the Gaussian mass concentrates at zero.  Equations
(17)--(18) give \(f_x=\widetilde f_x\) almost everywhere, hence everywhere
for their continuous \(H^\beta\) representatives.

For \(|u|\le\delta\), equations (10) and (16), together with the nonzero
denominator established above, yield
\[
 \widehat q_x(u)
 =\widehat f_x(u)\frac{G_{x,\vartheta}(u,0)}{F_{x,\vartheta}(u,0)}
 =\widehat{\widetilde f}_x(u)
   \frac{G_{x,\vartheta'}(u,0)}{F_{x,\vartheta'}(u,0)}
 =\widehat{\widetilde q}_x(u).                                   \tag{19}
\]
The domination \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) makes both signed densities integrable,
and their common compact support makes their transforms entire.  The
Taylor-series and Gaussian-convolution arguments used in (16)--(18) therefore
give \(q_x=\widetilde q_x\).  This holds for every cell \(x\).  Together with
(4), the limiting tuples have the same target function.

Finally, continuity of \(\vartheta\mapsto\mu_\vartheta\) from
\(\textnormal{lem:exact-class-compactness}\) and (3) imply
\[
 \|\mu_{\vartheta_k}-\mu_{\vartheta'_k}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \longrightarrow
 \|\mu_\vartheta-\mu_{\vartheta'}\|_{L^\infty(I)}=0,
\]
contradicting (2).  Hence \(\omega_n\to0\).  The compactness contradiction
is qualitative and supplies no numerical modulus or \(O(r_n)\) conclusion.

proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(P^{(0)},P^{(1)}\in\mathcal M\) induce the same observed-data law, and fix \(x\in\mathcal X\). By \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\), \(p_x\ge p_{\min}>0\), so conditioning on \(X=x\) is well defined and the common observed law determines both \(F_x\) and \(G_x\).

We first derive, rather than assume, a common protected neighborhood. For either candidate law, either \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and every real \(v\), the elementary inequality \(|e^{iz}-1|\le |z|\) for real \(z\), followed by H\"older's inequality and \(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\phi_j(v)|
 &\ge 1-|\phi_j(v)-1|\\
 &\ge 1-E_P\!\left[|e^{ivU_j}-1|\right]\\
 &\ge 1-|v|E_P|U_j|\\
 &\ge 1-|v|\{E_P|U_j|^{q_e}\}^{1/q_e}\\
 &\ge 1-|v|M_e^{1/q_e}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the fourth line is valid because the enlarged model has \(q_e>1\). Since \(M_e>0\), define
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}>0,
 \qquad c_*=\frac12,
 \qquad
 \delta=\min\left\{\frac{\nu_*}{2},\frac{1}{4B_A}\right\}>0.
\]
It follows that \(|\phi_j(v)|\ge c_*\) whenever \(|v|\le\nu_*\). On the other hand, \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) and the fact that \(f_x\) is a conditional density imply, for \(|w|\le2\delta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\widehat f_x(w)-1|
 &\le \int_{\mathcal A}|e^{iwa}-1|f_x(a)\,da\\
 &\le |w|\int_{\mathcal A}|a|f_x(a)\,da\\
 &\le B_A|w|\le\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(|\widehat f_x(w)|\ge1/2\) on \([-2\delta,2\delta]\). If \(|u|,|t|\le\delta\), then \(|u+t|\le2\delta\) and \(|u|,|t|\le\nu_*\). The probability-channel identity from \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\) consequently yields
\[
 |F_x(u,t)|
 =|\widehat f_x(u+t)|\,|\phi_1(u)|\,|\phi_2(t)|
 \ge \frac18>0.
\]
This proves the common near-origin nonvanishing needed below without any separately assumed spectral modulus.

The same moment calculation gives \(E_P|U_2|<\infty\), while \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) gives \(|A|\le B_A\) almost surely. Dominated differentiation is therefore valid at \(t=0\) in both the conditional expectation defining \(F_x(u,t)\) and the factorized expression. Define the observed logarithmic derivative, with \(\partial_t\log F_x\) interpreted as \((\partial_tF_x)/F_x\), by
\[
 D_x(u):=
 \frac{\left.\partial_tF_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}}{F_x(u,0)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
\]
Differentiating the factorization from \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\) and dividing by its nonzero value gives
\[
 D_x(u)
 =\frac{\widehat f_x'(u)}{\widehat f_x(u)}
  +\frac{\phi_2'(0)}{\phi_2(0)}.
\]
Characteristic-function normalization gives \(\phi_2(0)=1\). The finite first moment established above permits differentiation of \(\phi_2\) at zero, and \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\) gives
\[
 \phi_2'(0)=iE_P[U_2]=0.
\]
Consequently every candidate satisfies the observed ordinary differential equation
\[
 \widehat f_x'(u)=D_x(u)\widehat f_x(u),
 \qquad \widehat f_x(0)=\int_{\mathcal A}f_x(a)\,da=1,
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
\]
For the two candidate laws, the observed function \(D_x\) is the same. Since each candidate transform is nonzero on this interval, the ratio
\[
 R_x(u)=\frac{\widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)}{\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u)}
\]
satisfies \(R_x'(u)=0\) and \(R_x(0)=1\). Hence
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)=\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
\]
Only \(\phi_2\) was differentiated, so no location normalization on \(U_1\) has been used.

We next extend this equality without imposing global nonvanishing of either error transform. Let \(h=f_x^{(1)}-f_x^{(0)}\). Then \(h\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) and \(h\) is supported on \(\mathcal A=[-B_A,B_A]\). For every \(z\in\mathbb C\), absolute convergence and Tonelli's theorem give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 H(z)
 &:=\int_{\mathcal A}e^{iza}h(a)\,da\\
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz)^k}{k!}
       \int_{\mathcal A}a^kh(a)\,da,
\end{aligned}
\]
because
\[
 \int_{\mathcal A}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{|za|^k}{k!}|h(a)|\,da
 \le e^{|z|B_A}\|h\|_1<\infty.
\]
Thus \(H\) is entire. Its restriction to the real interval \((-\delta,\delta)\) is zero by the preceding local equality, so every derivative at zero is zero. The displayed everywhere-convergent power series then gives \(H(z)=0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb C\). In particular, the two density transforms agree on all real frequencies.

For the marked channel, \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\), evaluated at \((u,0)\), and the already proved nonvanishing give, for each candidate law,
\[
 \widehat q_x(u)
 =\widehat f_x(u)\frac{G_x(u,0)}{F_x(u,0)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
\]
The right-hand side is common to the two candidates because their observed channels and their recovered \(\widehat f_x\)'s are common. Therefore
\[
 \widehat q_x^{(1)}(u)=\widehat q_x^{(0)}(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
\]
To justify analytic continuation in this signed channel, \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcome}\) imply \(|Y|=|Y(A)|\le B_Y\) almost surely. Conditional Jensen's inequality hence gives \(|m_x(a)|\le B_Y\) for \(f_x(a)\,da\)-almost every \(a\), and the definition \(q_x=m_xf_x\) yields
\[
 |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\quad\text{almost everywhere},
 \qquad
 \|q_x\|_1\le B_Y.
\]
Moreover \(q_x\) is supported on \(\mathcal A\) because \(f_x\) is. Applying the same absolutely convergent power-series argument to \(q_x^{(1)}-q_x^{(0)}\) shows that the local equality of marked transforms extends to all \(z\in\mathbb C\).

For completeness, global equality of the transforms implies equality of the underlying functions. If \(h\) denotes either the difference of the two \(f_x\)'s or the difference of the two \(q_x\)'s, then \(h\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) and \(\widehat h(t)=0\) for all real \(t\). For \(\epsilon>0\), put
\[
 g_\epsilon(v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}
 e^{-v^2/(2\epsilon)}.
\]
The Gaussian integral and Fubini's theorem, whose absolute-integrability premise follows from \(h\in L^1\) and \(e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\in L^1\), give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (h*g_\epsilon)(a)
 &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}
 e^{-ita}\widehat h(t)e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\,dt=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Also,
\[
 \|h*g_\epsilon-h\|_1
 \le\int_{\mathbb R}g_\epsilon(v)
       \|h(\cdot-v)-h\|_1\,dv\longrightarrow0.
\]
Indeed, translation continuity is first immediate for compactly supported step functions and then follows for every \(L^1\) function by \(L^1\) approximation; splitting the last integral at any fixed small \(|v|\) and using concentration of \(g_\epsilon\) at zero proves the limit. Since every convolution in the display is zero, \(h=0\) almost everywhere.

Finally, \(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), and the enlarged range \(\beta>1/2\) provide unique continuous representatives. Indeed, for either difference \(h\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat h(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
                 |\widehat h(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 <\infty,
\]
where the second factor is finite exactly because \(\beta>1/2\). Fourier inversion therefore supplies a continuous representative, and two continuous representatives equal almost everywhere only if they agree everywhere. Since \(x\) was arbitrary, the common observed law determines every \(f_x\) and \(q_x\). The proof used the errors only on the derived interval \([-\nu_*,\nu_*]\), so it remains valid when either error characteristic function has an open zero set away from zero.

proposed.statement: The map \(P\mapsto P_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is injective for \(\{(f_x,q_x):x\in\mathcal X\}\) over \(\mathcal M\). On a common neighborhood of zero, \(\left.\partial_t\log F_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}=\widehat f_x'(u)/\widehat f_x(u)+\phi_2'(0)=\widehat f_x'(u)/\widehat f_x(u)\), because \(\phi_2(0)=1\) and \(\phi_2'(0)=iE_P[U_2]=0\). Together with \(\widehat f_x(0)=1\), this derivative identity uniquely fixes the latent translation without a normalization on \(U_1\). Moreover, \(\widehat q_x(u)=\widehat f_x(u)G_x(u,0)/F_x(u,0)\). Compact support makes both recovered transforms entire, so the local formulas determine \(f_x\) and \(q_x\) globally even when either error transform has an open zero set away from zero.
